question.text: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = x \,\mathbf{i} -z \,\mathbf{j} + y\,\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 2\,\mathbf{i} + \cos (\pi t)\, \mathbf{j} + \sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,2).$
question.explanation:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C.$ It is given by the formula \[ \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 2, \qquad y = \cos (\pi t), \qquad z = \sin (\pi t). \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= x \,\mathbf{i} -z \,\mathbf{j} + y\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= 2\,\mathbf{i}-\sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} + \cos (\pi t) \,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\cos (\pi t))\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sin (\pi t))\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= 0\,\mathbf{i} -\pi\sin(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + \pi \cos (\pi t) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left(2\,\mathbf{i}-\sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} + \cos (\pi t) \,\mathbf{k}\right) \cdot \left( -\pi\sin(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + \pi \cos (\pi t) \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &=2\cdot 0 +(-\sin(\pi t)) \cdot (-\pi \sin (\pi t)) + \cos (\pi t) \cdot \pi \cos (\pi t) \\[5pt] &= \pi\sin^2 (\pi t) +\pi \cos^2 (\pi t) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r &= \int_{0}^{2} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{0}^{2} \pi \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \pi \big[ t \big]_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] &= \pi(2-0) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = -y \,\mathbf{i} +x\,\mathbf{j}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 2\cos (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} + 2\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,2).$
question.explanation:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C.$ It is given by the formula \[ \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 2\cos (\pi t), \qquad y = \sin (\pi t), \qquad z = 2. \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= -y \,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] &= -\sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + 2\cos (\pi t) \,\mathbf{j}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2\cos (\pi t))\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sin (\pi t))\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= -2\pi \sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \pi \cos (\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} +0 \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left(-\sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + 2\cos (\pi t) \,\mathbf{j} \right) \cdot \left(-2\pi \sin (\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \pi \cos (\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} +0 \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &= -\sin (\pi t) \cdot (-2\pi \sin (\pi t)) + 2\cos (\pi t) \cdot \pi \cos (\pi t) + 0 \cdot 0 \\[5pt] &= 2\pi\sin^2 (\pi t) + 2 \pi \cos^2 (\pi t) \\[5pt] &= 2\pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r &= \int_{0}^{2} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{0}^{2} 2\pi \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 2\pi \big[ t \big]_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] &= 2\pi(2-0) \\[5pt] &= 4\pi \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = (y-x)\,\mathbf{i}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} +( t^3-t)\,\mathbf{j} + \sin(2\pi t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,1).$
question.explanation:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C.$ It is given by the formula \[ \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t^2-t, \qquad y = t^3-t, \qquad z = \sin(2\pi t). \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &=(y-x)\,\mathbf{i} \\[5pt] &= (t^3-t -t^2+t) \,\mathbf{i} \\[5pt] &= (t^3-t^2) \,\mathbf{i}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^3-t)\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\, \sin(2\pi t)\, )\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (2t-1) \,\mathbf{i} +(3t^2-1) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\pi\cos(2\pi t) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left(\,(t^3-t^2) \,\mathbf{i}\, \right) \cdot \left(\, (2t-1) \,\mathbf{i} +(3t^2-1) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\pi\cos(2\pi t) \, \mathbf{k} \,\right) \\[5pt] &= (t^3-t^2) \cdot (2t-1) + 0\cdot(3t^2-1) + 0 \cdot 2\cos(2\pi t) \\[5pt] &= 2 t^4-t^3-2t^3+t^2\\[5pt] & = 2t^4-3t^3+t^2. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} \left( \, 2t^4-3t^3+t^2\, \right) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{2t^5}{5}-\dfrac {3t^4}{4} +\dfrac {t^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac2{5}-\dfrac{3}{4}+ \dfrac{1}{3}\right)- \left( 0\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac1{60} \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = x \,\mathbf{i} - z\,\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + (t^3-t^2)\,\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,1).$
question.explanation:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C.$ It is given by the formula \[ \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x =t^2-t, \qquad y = t^3-t^2, \qquad z = 1. \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= x \,\mathbf{i} - z\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] &= (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} - 1 \,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}( t^3-t^2)\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(1)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (2t-1)\,\mathbf{i} +(3t^2-2t) \, \mathbf{j}+ 0 \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left((t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} - \,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left( (2t-1)\,\mathbf{i} +(3t^2-2t) \, \mathbf{j} \right) \\[5pt] &=(t^2-t) \cdot (2t-1) + 0 \cdot (3t^2-2t) + (-1)\cdot 0 \\[5pt] %&= (t^2-t) \cdot (2t-1) \\[5pt] &= (t^2-t)(2t-1). \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} (t^2-t)(2t-1) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{(t^2-t)^2}2 \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= (0-0)\\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = z \,\mathbf{j} - y\,\mathbf{k}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = (t^2- t)\,\mathbf{i} + \cos (2\pi t)\, \mathbf{j} + \sin (2\pi t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,1)$
question.explanation:
The circulation $\Gamma$ measures the total work done by a force $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle along a closed curve $C.$ It is given by the formula \[ \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t^2-t, \qquad y = \cos (2\pi t), \qquad z = \sin (2\pi t). \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= z \,\mathbf{j} -y\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \sin (2\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} - \cos (2\pi t) \,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\cos (2\pi t))\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sin (2\pi t))\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (2t-1)\,\mathbf{i} -2\pi\sin(2\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\pi \cos (2\pi t) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left(\sin (2\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} - \cos (2\pi t) \,\mathbf{k}\right) \cdot \left( (2t-1)\,\mathbf{i} -2\pi\sin(2\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\pi \cos (2\pi t) \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &=0\cdot (2t-1) +\sin (2\pi t) \cdot (-2\pi \sin (2\pi t)) + (-\cos (2\pi t)) \cdot 2\pi \cos (2\pi t) \\[5pt] &= -2\pi\sin^2 (2\pi t) - 2\pi \cos^2 (2\pi t) \\[5pt] &= -2\pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \Gamma = \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf r &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\ &= \int_{0}^{1} (-2\pi) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= -2\pi \big[ t \big]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= -2\pi(1-0) \\[5pt] &= -2\pi \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = (t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + (t-t^3) \, \mathbf{j} + (2t^2-2t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,1).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\,\mathbf{i}+x\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t^2-t, \qquad y = t-t^3, \qquad z = 2t^2-2t. \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= y\,\mathbf{i}+x\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (t-t^3)\,\mathbf{i}+(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t-t^3)\,\mathbf{j} - \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t^2-2t)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= (2t-1) \, \mathbf{i} + (1-3t^2) \, \mathbf{j} + (4t-2) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left( (t-t^3)\,\mathbf{i}+(t^2-t) \,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left( (2t-1) \, \mathbf{i} + (1-3t^2) \, \mathbf{j} + (4t-2) \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &= (t-t^3) \cdot (2t-1) + 0 \cdot (1-3t^2) + (t^2-t) \cdot (4t-2) \\[5pt] &= t - 4 t^2 + 5 t^3 - 2 t^4. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} (t - 4t^2 + 5t^3 - 2t^4) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{4t^3}{3} + \dfrac{5t^3}{4} - \dfrac{2t^5}{5} \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{5}{4} - \dfrac{2}{5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{60} \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = (t^2+t)\,\mathbf{i} + (t^3+t^2) \, \mathbf{j} + (2t^2+2t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [-1,0).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = y\,\mathbf{i} + z\,\mathbf{j} + x\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that \[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t^2+t, \qquad y = t^3+t^2, \qquad z = 2t^2+2t. \]

So, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & = y\,\mathbf{i} + z\,\mathbf{j} + x\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] & = (t^3 + t^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (2t^2+2t)\,\mathbf{j} + (t^2+t)\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2+t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^3+t^2)\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t^2+2t)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] & = (2t+1) \, \mathbf{i} + (3t^2+2t) \, \mathbf{j} + (4t+2) \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) & = \left( (t^3 + t^2)\,\mathbf{i} + (2t^2+2t)\,\mathbf{j} + (t^2+t)\,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left( (2t+1) \, \mathbf{i} + (3t^2+2t) \, \mathbf{j} + (4t+2) \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] & = (t^3+t^2)(2t+1) + (2t^2+2t)(3t^2+2t) + (t^2+t)(4t+2) \\[5pt] & = 2t + 11t^2 + 17t^3 + 8t^4. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{0} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{0} (2t + 11t^2 + 17t^3 + 8t^4) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[t^2 + \dfrac{11}{3}t^3 + \dfrac{17}{4}t^4 + \dfrac{8}{5}t^5 \right]_{-1}^{0}\\[5pt] &= 0-\left(1 - \dfrac{11}{3} + \dfrac{17}{4} - \dfrac{8}{5}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{60} \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \sin(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + \cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [-1,1).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\,\mathbf{i}+x\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \cos(\pi t), \qquad y = \sin(\pi t), \qquad z = \cos(\pi t). \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &= y\,\mathbf{i}+x\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &=\sin(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i}+\cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\cos(\pi t))\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sin(\pi t))\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\cos(\pi t))\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &=-\pi \sin(\pi t)\, \mathbf{i} +\pi \cos(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} - \pi \sin(\pi t)\, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left( \sin(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i}+\cos(\pi t) \,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left(-\pi \sin(\pi t)\, \mathbf{i} +\pi \cos(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} - \pi \sin(\pi t)\, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &= \sin(\pi t) \cdot(- \pi \sin(\pi t)) + 0 \cdot \pi \cos(\pi t)+ \cos(\pi t) \cdot (-\pi \sin(\pi t)) \\[5pt] &=- \pi \sin(\pi t)\cos(\pi t)-\pi \sin^2(\pi t). \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} (- \pi \sin(\pi t)\cos(\pi t)-\pi \sin^2(\pi t)) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=- \int_{-1}^{1} \left(\pi \sin(\pi t)\cos(\pi t)+\dfrac{\pi}{2} \left(1-\cos(2\pi t)\right)\right) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=- \left[ \dfrac{\sin^2(\pi t)}{2}+ \dfrac{\pi t}{2} - \dfrac{\sin(2\pi t)}{4} \right]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &=- \left[ 0+ \dfrac{\pi }{2}+0 -\left(0-\dfrac{\pi}{2}+0 \right)\right]\\[5pt] &=- \pi \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = (t^3-t)\,\mathbf{i} + (2t^2+1) \, \mathbf{j} + (t^2-1)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [-1,1).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = y\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j} + yz\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that \[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t^3-t, \qquad y = 2t^2+1, \qquad z = t^2-1. \]

So, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & = y\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j} + yz\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] & = (2t^2+1)\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j} + (2t^2+1)(t^2-1)\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] & = (2t^2+1)\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j} + (2t^4-t^2-1)\,\mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^3-t)\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t^2+1)\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^2-1)\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] & = (3t^2-1) \, \mathbf{i} + 4t \, \mathbf{j} + 2t \, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) & = \left( (2t^2+1)\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j} + (2t^4-t^2-1)\,\mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left( (3t^2-1) \, \mathbf{i} + 4t \, \mathbf{j} + 2t \, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] & = (2t^2+1)(3t^2-1) + 3(4t) + (2t^4-t^2-1)(2t) \\[5pt] & = -1 + 10t + t^2 - 2t^3 + 6t^4 + 4t^5. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} (-1 + 10t + t^2 - 2t^3 + 6t^4 + 4t^5) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left[-t + 5t^2 + \dfrac{1}{3}t^3 - \dfrac{1}{2}t^4 + \dfrac{6}{5}t^5 + \dfrac{2}{3}t^6\right]_{-1}^{1}\\[5pt] & = \left(-1 + 5 + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{6}{5} + \dfrac{2}{3}\right) -\left(1 + 5 - \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{6}{5} + \dfrac{2}{3}\right) \\[5pt] & = -2 + \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{12}{5} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{16}{15} \end{align*}

question.text: Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i} + \sin(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\sin(\pi t)\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [-1,1).$ Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=2y\,\mathbf{i}-2x\,\mathbf{j} + e^{z-2y}\,\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral \[ \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \cos(\pi t), \qquad y = \sin(\pi t), \qquad z =2\sin(\pi t). \]

So,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) &=2 y\,\mathbf{i}-2x\,\mathbf{j} + e^{z-2y}\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= 2\sin(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i}- 2\cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} + e^{2\sin(\pi t)- 2\sin(\pi t)}\,\mathbf{k}\\[5pt] &= 2\sin(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i}- 2\cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} . \end{align*}

Computing $\mathbf r'(t),$ we get

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\cos(\pi t))\,\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sin(\pi t))\,\mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2\sin(\pi t))\,\mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= -\pi \sin(\pi t)\, \mathbf{i} +\pi \cos(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\pi \cos(\pi t)\, \mathbf{k}. \end{align*}

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r' (t) &= \left( 2\sin(\pi t)\,\mathbf{i}- 2\cos(\pi t)\,\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k} \right) \cdot \left(-\pi \sin(\pi t)\, \mathbf{i} +\pi \cos(\pi t) \, \mathbf{j} + 2\pi \cos(\pi t)\, \mathbf{k} \right) \\[5pt] &=2 \sin(\pi t) \cdot (-\pi \sin(\pi t) ) - 2\cos(\pi t) \cdot \pi \cos(\pi t)+ 1 \cdot 2\pi \cos(\pi t) \\[5pt] &= -2\pi \sin^2(\pi t) - 2\pi \cos^2(\pi t) + 2\pi \cos(\pi t) \\[5pt] &= -2\pi +2\pi \cos(\pi t) . \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \mathbf F(r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t) \; \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} (-2\pi +2\pi \cos(\pi t)) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \big[ -2\pi t +2 \sin(\pi t) \big]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &= (-2\pi(1)+0 ) - (-2\pi(-1)+0 ) \\[5pt] &= -4\pi \end{align*}

question.text: Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate \[ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}, \] where $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle y, \: 2yz, \: -z^2+1 \rangle,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the half-cone $z=-\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and the plane $z=-3.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation

\[ z = g(x,y) = -3. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(-3) = 0 \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(-3) = 0 \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle y, \: 2yz, \: -z^2+1 \rangle \Big|_{z=-3} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{-6y}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{-8}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -y \cdot 0 - (-6y) \cdot 0 - 8 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D -8 \: \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=9$ with radius $3$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

\[ x = r \cos\theta, \qquad y = r \sin\theta, \qquad \textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta, \]

we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D -8 \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{3} -8 \cdot r \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= -8 \int_{0}^{2\pi} \, \textrm{d}\theta \cdot \int_{0}^{3} r \, \textrm{d}r \\[5pt] &= -8 \big[ \theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \cdot \left[ \dfrac{r^2}2 \right]_{r=0}^{r=3} \\[5pt] &= -8 (2\pi-0) \cdot \left(\dfrac 92 - 0\right) \\[5pt] &= -72\pi. \end{align*}

question.text: Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate \[ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}, \] where $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle x+y, \: -x+y, \: -2z \rangle,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^2+(y+1)^2.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the paraboloid $z=(x-1)^2+(y+1)^2.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation

\[ z = g(x,y) = (x-1)^2+(y+1)^2. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}((x-1)^2+(y+1)^2) = 2(x-1) \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}((x-1)^2+(y+1)^2) = 2(y+1) \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle x+y, \: -x+y, \: - 2z \rangle \Big|_{z=(x-1)^2+(y+1)^2} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{x+y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{-x+y}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{-2(x-1)^2 - 2(y+1)^2}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -(x+y) \cdot 2(x-1) - (-x+y) \cdot 2(y+1) - 2((x-1)^2+(y+1)^2) \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D 2\big( (x+y)(1-x) + (x-y)(y+1) - (x-1)^2 - (y+1)^2\big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D 4(-x^2-y^2+2x-y-1) \: \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

\[ x = r \cos\theta, \qquad y = r \sin\theta, \qquad \textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta, \]

we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D 4(-x^2-y^2+2x-y-1) \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2\pi} 4(-r^2 + 2r\cos\theta - r\sin\theta - 1) \cdot r \: \textrm{d}\theta \: \textrm{d}r\\[5pt] &= 4\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \big(-r^3 + 2r^2\cos\theta - r^2\sin\theta - r\big) \: \textrm{d}\theta \: \textrm{d}r\\[5pt] &= 4\int_{0}^{1} \left[ -r^3 \theta + 2r^2 \cos\theta + r^2\cos\theta - r\theta\right]_{0}^{2\pi}\: \textrm{d}r\\[5pt] &= 4\int_{0}^{1} \left( -2\pi r^3 - 2\pi r\right)\: \textrm{d}r\\[5pt] &= -8\pi \left[ -\dfrac{r^4}{4} - \dfrac{r^2}{2}\right]_0^1\\[5pt] &= -8\pi \left( -\dfrac 14 - \dfrac 12 \right)\\[5pt] &= -6\pi. \end{align*}

question.text: Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate \[ \displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}, \] where $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} = \langle -y, \: z, \: -2x \rangle,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}. \]

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder $x^2+y^2=1$ and the plane $z=2+2x-y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation

\[ z = g(x,y) = 2+2x-y. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(2+2x-y) = 2 \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(2+2x-y) = -1 \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle -y, \: z, \: -2x \rangle \Big|_{z=2+2x-y} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{-y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{2+2x-y}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{-2x}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

So, we have

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -(-y) \cdot (2) - (2+2x-y) \cdot (-1) - 2x \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( 2y + 2+2x-y - 2x \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (2+y) \: \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

\[ x = r \cos\theta, \qquad y = r \sin\theta, \qquad \textrm{d}A = r \, \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta, \]

we obtain

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D (2+y) \: \textrm{d}A &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} (2 + r \sin\theta) \cdot r \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} 2r + r^2 \sin\theta \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left[ r^2 + \dfrac{r^3}{3}\sin\theta \right]_0^1 \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \left( 1 + \dfrac 13 \sin\theta\right) \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] &= \left[ \theta - \dfrac 13\cos\theta \right]_{0}^{2\pi}\\[5pt] &= 2\pi. \end{align*}

Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

\[ z = g(x,y) = x^2 - y^2. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2-y^2) = 2x \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2-y^2) = -2y \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}{:}$

\begin{align} \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \, \Big|_{z=g(x,y)} &= \langle y, \: x, \: 2 \rangle \Big|_{z=x^2-y^2} \\[5pt] &= \big\langle y, \: x, \: 2 \big\rangle \\[5pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{x}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{2}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( - y \cdot (2x) - x \cdot (-2y) + 2 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D 2\, \textrm{d}A, \end{align*}

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.
